scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Suleiman Aga is classified as a subclass of Karsilamas, a traditional folk dance spread across Northwest Turkey, Greece, and the wider Balkan and Ottoman historic region.
The wider dance tradition was carried across regions by populations including Anatolian Greek immigrants, maintaining deep roots from Persia to Serbia.
on_screen: Map: Turkey · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Derived from the Turkish word meaning 'encounter, welcoming, greeting', the dance functions as a social face-to-face interaction celebrating communal bonds during weddings and regional festivals.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a couple dance where two people face each other.
Dancers move rhythmically to the music without mandatory fixed figures, traditionally drawing from moves seen from elders.
The basic movement follows a 9/8 meter executed in four small steps with beat durations divided as 2+2+2+3.
Watch for Face-to-face greeting step.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Face-to-face couple positioning with fluid spatial interaction
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical foundation relies on a 9/8 time signature.

As part of the broader Karsilamas family, the music rhythmically controls the dancers' steps, varying in style and mood from bouncy and lively to smooth depending on the specific regional interpretation.
Listen for the zurna, davul, clear percussion, lute.
The pulse is 9/8 at about 130 beats a minute.
A rhythmic 9/8 metric structure defined by a 2+2+2+3 pulse driving dynamic melodic lines characteristic of Balkan and Anatolian folk music.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Suleiman Aga exists alongside numerous regional Karsilamas variants across Thrace, Macedonia, the Aegean islands, Merzifon, Edirne, Giresun, Taraklı, and Bilecik.
Classified as a subclass of Karsilamas, reflecting a lineage of Anatolian, Balkan, and Ottoman face-to-face couple dances.

Step 2: Step 2 (duration 2 counts): Small step matching rhythm

on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
